blocks.p: Rei walked to Senju along the river. It took him more than an hour, with the carrier on his shoulder and Kuga's weight shifting inside it at every step. The Sumida river runs east out of Kita in long slow bends, with a raised concrete embankment on each side and a path along the top. At night the path was nearly empty. A man in a sweat-soaked T-shirt jogged past with a small light on his chest. Further on, an old man sat on a folding stool with a fishing rod, a radio playing baseball quietly at his feet, though there could be nothing worth catching in that black water. The air smelled of mud and warm concrete.

Down in the streets on either side, the okuribi were burning. From the embankment Rei could see them as tiny orange points by the doorsteps, one here, two there, and families crouched beside them in summer clothes. A grandmother held a small child's hand over a flame to show him how close was safe. A man in a white shirt stood alone by his fire with his hands together and his head bowed, and did not move the whole time Rei was passing. The smoke from the burning hemp stalks drifted up over the river and made his eyes water.

He chose the node behind the Senju waterworks because it was the one Gin had marked smallest, in the back of the book, the way Gin marked the things he meant to come back to. Smallest tear. Most likely to let a living man back out. And he chose it because it was not in Kita. Somewhere along the river, with the carrier on his shoulder, he had felt the attention of the gutters slide off him. The rats watched Kita. They did not watch Senju. Gin's book had said to change the district, and for one night he had.

Okada was already there. She was kneeling at the edge of a concrete settling pool behind the pump house, where the overflow water lay dead still under the security lights. Big pipes ran along the wall behind her, humming. She had brought two things in a cool-box. One was a towel. The other, when she lifted the lid, was a long, pale, patterned snake that poured itself over her wrist without any hurry.

blocks.cap: A rat snake set across the sill

blocks.p: "Japanese rat snake," she said. "Not venomous. The venom isn't the point." She set it across the sill of the yard gate and dusted the concrete in front of it with a handful of dark earth from a paper bag. "Graveyard earth. It sharpens the snake at that one spot, gives us another forty minutes of good warning. Anything that tries to cross that gate, it strikes. It can't see what it's striking any better than we can. It just knows." She sat back on her heels. "It strikes people too. So when you come back, you come back here, at the water. Not through the gate. Route yourself." She rubbed the snake's head with one thumb. "Two hours, then it gets tired and starts snapping at its own side. We won't need two hours. Nobody holds a cat door past forty minutes."

While she set the snake, Rei sat on the edge of the pool with Gin's book open on his knees. It was open at the page he had read most often that month, a hand-drawn map of Kita's pockets. A pocket, as Gin used it, meant a fold in the veil, a small hidden space between the living world and the other side.

doc.title: Gin's book. Pockets. What they actually are
lines: A pocket is a stable fold in the membrane. A space between the living world and the Threshold where a practitioner can work without entity exposure. Time runs at about the same rate inside. Once you are in, entities cannot follow at standard capability. Good for training, for meeting people where the demon's monitoring cannot reach, for recovery.
Shallow. A standard fold. Entity-free. Exits where you entered. It takes a Vanguard to make a new one.
Mid-depth. Made by people who wanted to be near the Font. The Architect's processes are faintly legible. Arbiter rank to navigate. Can exit somewhere else in the living world if you know the mapping.
Deep. The floor is unstable. The Architect is close. Entities avoid it. The most dangerous thing here is the Architect. If the floor gives out under you, you come out next to the Threshold.
Beyond. Below the Threshold. No one in any record I can reach has come back from this depth with a coherent account.
Three pockets in Kita. One is the evidence archive itself, which is slightly larger inside than its floor plan. One is a manhole behind building 14B. The third I am not writing down.
I went into the deepest one twice. The second time I came out three districts away, six hours later. My archive entry from that day is the one that is slightly wrong.
Of the five I mapped, one has no depth marker. I stopped at the edge and did not go in. The needle points straight down when I hold it near the entrance.

What pockets are not. Safe from the Font. The Font is not an entity. It is the infrastructure, and the pockets are inside it. If it is paying attention to you, that attention follows you in. The pockets are safe from demons. They are not safe from the architect of the space everyone is living in. G.U.

blocks.p: Put simply, a pocket could hide a person from demons, but not from the Font, and the deeper the pocket, the closer it sat to the Architect. Rei had thought about the unmarked pocket all afternoon, the one where the needle pointed down. It went where he needed to go. It also went to the place nobody had come back from with their words in order, and even Gin had stopped at its edge. A pocket would hide him from the Healer. It would not hide him from the thing he was going to see. Nothing would. He shut the book and put it inside his shirt, against his skin, where he could feel its corner.
Before he closed it, Okada took out Gin's page on the sight scale. She read it and handed it back folded small. "Read it once more," she said. "So you know what's happening when it happens."

doc.title: Veil Sight. The Four Tiers
lines: I. E and D rank. The Grey Blur. Sensitivity without sight. Heaviness, wrongness, residue. No shape. About a fifth of the other side visible.
II. C and B rank. Shadows and Shape. The veil becomes visible. Shapes resolve into forms. Type and register readable. From here, entities see you back. Visibility goes both ways.
III. A and S rank. Full Dual Perception. Both worlds at once, fully populated. A street, plus everything that has died on it.
IV. SS and SSS rank. Structural Sight. The membrane itself is visible. No off switch. You adapt to it.
Thin spots raise every tier by one... and the entities see you the same amount more.
Gin, in the margin beside Rei's name. Presenting Sensitive with suppression running. Actual sight significantly higher. He calls it instinct. It is not instinct.

blocks.p: Rei took off his shoes and socks. The water was as warm as a bath at the edges and cool where he stood in it. It was two fingers deep over the concrete and flat as a sheet of glass. Okada unclipped the carrier. Kuga stepped out into the night as if he owned the waterworks. He looked at the pool with distaste, and then he let Rei lift him. He was heavier than he looked. Rei held him against his chest with both hands, the way the page said. Okada knelt at his shoulder with one hand an inch above the surface, ready to slap it into ripples if the cat decided wrong. A broken reflection is no door.
"Eyes," Okada said. "Don't look away. Whatever you see."
Rei looked into Kuga's eyes.

For a long time it was only a cat. Yellow eyes, a slit of black, one torn ear twitching at the sound of the pumps. Ten seconds. Twenty. Rei held on and did not blink. Then the weight in his hands changed, as if the cat had settled more deeply into itself. The eyes went half closed, and then fixed on his. The black of the pupil opened like a door being opened from the far side. It cost him at once. He felt a measure of himself drain out of him like warm water down a plughole. Behind Kuga's head, the waterworks stopped being the waterworks.

He had expected a lurch. Cold. The smell of a room shut up too long. He got none of it. He got Tokyo. The same August. The same Obon lanterns strung between the same poles. The same heat lying on the canal like a held breath. Only after a long moment did he understand that none of it was moving. The lanterns hung without swinging. The canal did not lap at its banks. The heat was only a memory of heat, laid over a place that had never had weather.

He went through the first layer so fast that he barely had time to be afraid of it. Kuga carried him through it the way an express train carries a passenger past a crowded platform without stopping. For a few heartbeats there was noise everywhere, and the noise was people. This was the Threshold, the nearest layer of the other side, where the newly dead arrive. Gin had written that the other side is not dark, it is loud, and here was the loud. The recent dead stood shoulder to shoulder like commuters in a station where the trains have stopped. They were confused. They kept turning, not yet sure which way they were meant to go. Mediums worked here. Exorcists worked here. A practitioner who touched this layer while worn out was at risk of possession. Nothing here hunted him. The crowd was simply so thick that it pressed in. Then the cat's gaze tipped, and the crowd fell away above Rei, and the quiet began.

blocks.cap: Kuga, and the Deep's copy of Kita

blocks.p: Below the Threshold was the Deep, and the Deep had made itself a copy of his district. It was Kita drawn by something that had only heard about it from others. The konbini on the corner was lit and empty. The rice balls behind the glass were the same four kinds, forever. The prices were right. The little hand-written apology taped to the broken coffee machine was right, down to its worn fold. When he tried the door with one bare foot, it opened onto more of the same street. There was no inside here. There was only the surface that things keep up to seem alive. Entities that have had time to develop culture, alliances, hierarchies, territories, agendas, Gin's book said of this layer. They have had time to develop opinions about visitors. Gin had been here twice. Both times on purpose.

Rei walked the way Gin had made him walk through the Archive, in Gin's strict order. North, then west, then the half step back that is not on any map. He kept Kuga's eyes the whole way. The false city let him pass, because to the far shore he was not yet a man. He was a draught under a door. He was the one cold thing in a room that did not know it had gone cold.
Then it noticed.

He felt the moment it happened, the way a person feels a stranger's eyes land on the back of his neck in a crowd. A small wrongness became an attention. Every lantern on the canal turned to face the same way, all at once and without swinging. They faced him. Rei's sight climbed on its own, as the page had said it would. Then it climbed again, because this whole place was one huge thin spot. The street became shapes. The shapes became forms, and he could read their registers, the feelings they fed on. From here, entities see you back. They did. The not-weather thickened. The konbini light behind him changed from a welcome into a witness. Okada had been right about the cat. To every instrument in Tokyo, he was a stray in a pool. To the things already here, he was perfectly visible.

He had come in as a draught, and the far shore had just learned to count. The number it had reached was one too many. Somewhere ahead, past the place where the streets stopped pretending, something that had been patient for a very long time put down what it was holding. And it began, without hurry, to come and see what was alive in its house.

Further in, the city gave up its pretending little by little, and that was worse than a clean edge would have been. First the writing went. The konbini signs, the ward notices, the lost-cat poster on the pole all kept their shape but lost their words, the way a name goes soft when it is said too many times. Then the depth went. Buildings became the idea of buildings, fronts that only believed they were fronts. Where two of them met, he could see there was nothing behind either one. Only the seam. Only the place the far shore had not bothered to imagine, because no living eye was ever meant to reach it.

Rei kept Gin's order, because it was the only handrail in a stairwell with no stairs. And at last he understood what the Archive had been. It was not a map of this place. It was a way of walking that this place would put up with. It was a politeness his brother had learned and written down small, so that one day Rei could be rude to a god without being killed on the doorstep.

He passed through what had been the canal. Now it was only the feeling of a long, cold absence. On the far side the houses were gone. There was only the standing. That was the only word he had for it. A field of upright attention, like a crowd seen from behind. None of it faced him. All of it faced inward, toward the centre, the way iron filings face a magnet. His sight had doubled now, full and steady, exactly as the page had promised. A street, plus everything that has died on it. Except the street was gone, and only the dead were left. Every soul who had ever stood in Kita in the dark and felt something with a name they almost knew pass overhead. He was walking through the inside of the dread his whole ward had felt all month without being able to say why.

And he could feel the slope again, the one he had seen from the kitchen floor. It was not under him now. It was in front of him, and it was everything. This was the third layer, the one Gin's diagram had drawn last and smallest, with no arrow showing a way out. The Font layer. Entities that reach it dissolve completely. Not painful. It is described as coming home. That is the part that frightens. Kuga's claws pricked through Rei's shirt, very gently, and Rei realised he had taken a step toward it without meaning to. He stopped. He held the cat's eyes and made himself stand still until the wanting passed. It did not pass. It only waited.
At the heart of the standing, where all of it leaned, there was a chair.

Not a throne. A chair. A plain one, the kind that belongs at a kitchen table, the kind he had sat in across from his brother on a thousand mornings. It was empty, and it was the loudest thing he had ever stood near. The Thirteenth Seat was neither occupied nor ruined. It was empty the way a bell is empty just after it has been struck. It was still ringing with the shape of the last holder, who had died out of it in 2009. The ringing was what thinned the wall. The ringing was what had been pulling at Gin. The ringing was the open mouth the Healer meant to fill.

blocks.cap: The man of light behind the empty chair, holding the door shut

blocks.p: Behind the chair, so close that the chair might have been his, stood the man.

He was made of light so cold that looking at it hurt Rei's teeth. He stood with his back to Rei and his back to the whole world, very straight and very still. His attention was fixed on something Rei could not see, and he was holding it shut. He did not turn. Gin's book had said he would not. It does not show its face. But Rei was close enough now to see what the light was wrapped around. The shoulders of a young man. Dark hair turning faintly see-through at the edges, where the light leaked out of him. A coat cut in a style nobody had used for a very long time. It was dark and plain and worn at the elbows, the kind of coat a man wears to work.

Rei was closer to the centre than any living man had ever stood. He took one more step, into the place where the standing leaned hardest. And the chair, the empty chair, turned its attention on him, all at once, the way the whole far shore had turned. Without words, in his own brother's way of speaking, it asked him what he thought he was.
